cards.title: Match the ad's exact promise to the landing page headline
cards.summary: Whatever specific, quantifiable claim won the click must be the first thing the visitor reads above the fold, or they bounce.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a paid-traffic landing page (Google or Meta) before or during a campaign to fix high bounce and low conversion from ad clicks.
steps: Pull the exact ad copy that generated the traffic — e.g. an ad promising 'Lose 6-20 lbs in 2-4 weeks' — and compare it word-for-word against the page headline.
Replace generic brand headlines ('Retreat to a new reality') with the same benefit and number the ad used, so the visitor instantly confirms they landed in the right place.
Treat the above-the-fold as the only section 100% of visitors see; the source states roughly 60% never scroll past it, so the core offer must live there.
If you run multiple ad angles, build a matching headline variant per angle rather than sending all traffic to one generic page.
Re-check congruence every time you rotate a new ad angle into the account.
caveats: The '60% never scroll' and '100% see above the fold' figures are the source's stated heuristics, not a universal measured benchmark for your store.

cards.title: Structure the above-the-fold anatomy for lead-gen pages
cards.summary: A high-converting hero section stacks a benefit headline, mechanism sub-headline, FUD reducers, a benefit-driven CTA, reinforcing imagery and social proof.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the top screen of a lead-gen, B2B or service landing page where the goal is form fills or booked calls.
steps: Write a headline that states the dream outcome ('lose fat fast'), not the company description.
Write a sub-headline that explains HOW you deliver the headline promise — unique mechanism, proprietary method or program steps — instead of repeating the headline.
Make the CTA button benefit-driven ('Gain muscle fast', 'Get thicker hair now') rather than generic ('Contact us', 'Schedule your free analysis'); the source calls 'contact us' overused and weak.
Place FUD reducers (fear, uncertainty, doubt) right beside the CTA: money-back guarantee, free trial, no surgery or pills, free shipping.
Use an image or video that reinforces the value prop (a transformation shot) rather than a generic facility photo.

Stack two forms of social proof — e.g. a real review plus a named-media quote — because the source says A/B testing showed two outperform one; a bare 'as seen on' logo row is overdone, so add an actual quote beneath the logo.
caveats: The two-social-proof and benefit-CTA claims are the presenter's agency's experience across 400+ pages, not a guaranteed lift for every niche.

cards.title: Remove navigation leaks on dedicated landing pages
cards.summary: Kill the top navigation bar on campaign pages so traffic cannot wander off to About, Explore or Blog before converting.
cards.use_when: Setting up any dedicated ad landing page (lead-gen, course, or single-offer ecommerce campaign page) where one conversion action is the goal.
steps: Decide the single conversion event for the page (form submit, call booking, add to cart) and make it the only exit you want.
Delete or visually suppress the site-wide navigation bar so visitors can't leave via About, Explore, Blog or category links.
Keep only the logo (linking home is optional) and the primary CTA in the header zone.
Verify on mobile, where the source focuses its audits, that the menu isn't hiding the CTA or pushing the offer below the fold.
Reserve full navigation for the main site and homepages where browsing is the goal — don't strip it everywhere.
caveats: This applies to dedicated paid-traffic landing pages; the source doesn't recommend removing navigation from a browsable storefront where category discovery drives revenue.

cards.title: Use the PAS framework in the post-hero pain section
cards.summary: For cold ad traffic, open the mid-page with Problem-Agitate-Solve so the copy names the struggle and immediately ties it to the unique solution.
cards.use_when: Writing the section right below the hero on a cold-traffic landing page (Meta/Google) where visitors don't know your brand yet.
steps: Place a pain-point section directly after the hero — the source's page framework puts pain right below the value prop.
Name the problem the visitor already feels (e.g. thinning hair in the mirror, shedding).
Agitate it briefly to raise emotional stakes without turning to fear-mongering.
Immediately pivot to the solve: your unique mechanism and how it resolves the specific pain.
Avoid pages that only list pain points with no solution attached — the source calls the pain-only version a common miss.
Use AI copy prompts only as a first draft, then edit for your actual mechanism and claims.
caveats: The source says its own AI-generated examples were placeholders; replace fabricated stats and claims with real, compliant ones before publishing.

cards.title: Make headlines readable on their own
cards.summary: Assume visitors read only headlines, so every section headline must communicate the benefit without the body copy.
cards.use_when: Editing landing page section headlines and CTA lead-ins, or diagnosing pages with vague headers like 'Analysis first' or 'Ready for your first step?'
steps: Read each headline in isolation and ask whether it names a concrete benefit or reason to act; rewrite anything a skimmer can't decode.
Write section headlines as benefit statements, not internal labels or rhetorical questions ('Ready for your first step?' gives no why).
Repeat the primary CTA button throughout every critical section rather than once at the bottom — the source claims more buttons increase conversion likelihood.
Compress over-long body copy (the source flags 8-line paragraphs as pushing key content below the fold) to 2-3 sentences max per block.
Sanity-check with the source's 80/20 rule: assume ~20% read copy and 80% scan, so headlines and visuals must carry the message.
caveats: The 20/80 read-vs-scan split and 'more buttons = more conversion' are the presenter's stated heuristics, not universal measured facts.

cards.title: Add a closing recap section at the page bottom
cards.summary: Treat the footer area as a mini above-the-fold that recaps value, restates the offer and reduces doubt one final time.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing the bottom of a lead-gen or course landing page where drop-off happens before the last CTA.
steps: Create a 'closer' block modeled on the hero: final value recap, three value props, CTA button, FUD reducers and an image, video or form.
Give one final reason to act today instead of a weak line like 'Want to know more?'.
Repeat the benefit-driven CTA that matches the hero button so the page ends on the same action.
Include the form or booking element inside the closer to capture visitors who scrolled the whole way.
Keep it visually distinct as a contained block so it reads as a deliberate summary, not stray footer links.
caveats: The source describes this as its own framework, not an A/B-validated result.

cards.title: Offer one core action per lead-gen page
cards.summary: Competing offers split attention; pick a single conversion action and reduce up-front friction.
cards.use_when: Auditing a lead-gen page that shows two CTAs (e.g. 'schedule a free analysis' and 'get your free guide') or requires booking a call immediately.
steps: Count the distinct offers and CTAs on the page; if there's more than one core action, cut down to the single best-converting action.
For cold Meta/Google traffic, lower up-front friction by collecting simple info via a form instead of demanding a full call booking.
Move a call-booking calendar to a later step after the lead is captured, if you still want a call.
Ensure the remaining CTA is benefit-driven, not a generic service label.
Re-audit after edits to confirm no secondary offer (guide, newsletter, second form) has crept back in.
caveats: The presenter's preference for forms over instant call booking is a positioning choice for cold traffic, not a rule that works for every funnel or high-intent offer.

cards.title: Convert transactional course pages into outcome-driven offers
cards.summary: Sell the transformation and career outcome, not the format and duration, then stack value so the price feels like a no-brainer.
cards.use_when: Writing the above-the-fold and offer sections of a digital product, course or certificate sales page.
steps: Replace format-style titles ('Dual health and life coach certificate', 'Digital imaging technician course') with the end outcome buyers care about ('Land six-figure DIT gigs, travel the world, work on global sets').
Move transactional specs (online, self-paced, 5 months, 3-5 hours/week) out of the hero and into supporting detail.
Enumerate exactly what's included — modules, video counts, completion certificates, module-by-module contents — so the offer is fully legible.
Apply value stacking: assign a dollar value to each bonus and module, show the total, and present the bundled price against that stack.
Position the whole package as one price for a large list of inclusions, whether the ticket is high or low.
Keep the presentation concrete rather than a vague 'who is this for' laundry list.
caveats: The 'felt like a no-brainer' outcome is the source's framing from its own client work, not a measured conversion result.

cards.title: Diagnose ecommerce homepage by View Product Rate
cards.summary: The homepage's job is to move visitors to product pages, so optimize for the share who view a product.
cards.use_when: Reviewing store homepage performance when category and product page traffic is under target.
steps: Measure View Product Rate — the presenter calls it the most under-indexed metric on the store homepages it audits.
Rewrite the homepage headline to state the customer benefit instead of burying it in sub-copy no one reads.
Choose imagery that reinforces the emotional promise (smiling pets for happy-pet positioning, not under-the-weather shots).
Replace text-only dropdowns with icons or images beside category items; the source reports a 15% conversion lift from an image-navigation A/B test for a pet client.
Keep the number of top-level menu items at or under seven to avoid analysis paralysis and site exits.
Retest menu imagery per niche before rolling out store-wide.
caveats: The 15% lift and 'seven items' threshold are source-specific A/B and agency observations, not universal benchmarks — validate on your own traffic.

cards.title: Fix PDP image and information hierarchy above the fold
cards.summary: Expose thumbnails, lead with the title, surface reviews and keep add-to-cart with FUD reducers in the first screen.
cards.use_when: Restructuring an ecommerce product page and its above-the-fold layout.
steps: Replace hidden carousel dots with visible image thumbnails so shoppers see the full gallery immediately.
Order the hierarchy title-first, then reviews — not reviews below the title — because on landing pages reviews are placed first.
Fit as much purchase-critical info above the fold as possible; the source draws a 'red line' and says everything above it should be visible without scrolling.
Keep the Add to Cart button and its FUD reducers together: money-back guarantee, warranty, free shipping.
Break long body copy into icon-supported benefit bullets, since the source assumes most visitors scan rather than read.
Confirm the layout on mobile as well as desktop.
caveats: Hierarchy preferences (reviews above title) come from the source's framework and testing, not a universal rule for every category.

cards.title: Don't make shoppers do bundle math
cards.summary: State the exact dollar saving in the bundle headline instead of showing only a discounted price.
cards.use_when: Designing bundle offers and quantity-break pricing on an ecommerce product page.
steps: Identify bundle options (2-pack, 3-pack) and calculate the exact amount saved per bundle.
Put the saving in the bundle title itself — '3-Pack: Save $20', 'One pack save €10, Two pack save €22' — rather than hiding it in small price text.
Make the saving visually prominent on mobile; the source flags discounts that are invisible on a phone as a key miss.
Compare bundles side by side so the shopper sees the escalating saving without arithmetic.
A/B test headline saving amounts against standard discounted-price displays.
caveats: The source reports testing this but does not publish a specific lift figure; treat as a hypothesis to validate on your own store.

cards.title: Turn dense product copy into scannable visuals
cards.summary: Break long product-information blocks into icon-driven, image-led value props that skimmers actually consume.
cards.use_when: Rewriting a product page or landing page section that currently uses large paragraphs of specification text.
steps: Identify the biggest blocks of undifferentiated text on the page — specs, features, materials.
Extract the benefit of each feature and present it as a short icon-plus-line item.
Pair each benefit with imagery so the section is visual rather than prose.
Repeat this treatment across the page's value prop sections rather than one hero-only fix.
Keep some text for the minority who read, but lead with scannable structure.
caveats: The read/scan split behind this is the source's stated heuristic, not a measured benchmark.

cards.title: Judge best-practice tactics by impact, not checkbox compliance
cards.summary: Implementing a tactic without making it impactful still fails; e.g. a generic testimonial or generic 'as seen on' logos solve nothing.
cards.use_when: Auditing a page that claims to follow best practices (testimonials, logos, guarantees) but still converts poorly.
steps: List each 'best practice' element on the page and ask what specific doubt or desire it resolves.
Replace generic testimonials with ones that mirror the core value prop and outcome.
Replace bare 'as seen on' logo rows with an actual quote from the featured source.
Replace filler headlines like 'Analysis first, then focus' with benefit-driven statements.
If an element adds no impact, remove or rework it rather than keeping it for appearance.
Apply this filter to every section before adding new tactics.
caveats: This is the presenter's critique from auditing client pages, not an empirical study; use judgment per brand.

cards.title: Reuse ad-to-page congruence and hero anatomy for digital product pages
cards.summary: The lead-gen hero framework (benefit headline, mechanism sub-headline, FUD reducers, CTA, social proof) transfers to course and product pages.
cards.use_when: Adapting a proven lead-gen hero structure to a digital product or course sales page during a redesign.
steps: Overlay the same anatomy on the course page: outcome headline, how-we-deliver sub-headline, two social proofs, benefit CTA, doubt reducers.
Add the ad's exact promise to the hero when the course page receives paid traffic.
Update CTA copy from transactional ('Enroll now') to outcome-driven where it fits the brand.
Place guarantee or refund terms close to the purchase button as the FUD reducer.
Roll the same structure down the page into each value section rather than only fixing the hero.
caveats: The source notes overlap between B2B, digital-product and ecommerce pages but presents this as its own framework, not a validated universal layout.

input.text:
07-LPG / landing pages and funnels

Goes here. A diagnostic breakdown of common landing page conversion killers across B2B, digital products, and e-commerce, offering actionable CRO (Conversion Rate Optimization) fixes such as optimizing the above-the-fold, restructuring navigation, and visualizing product bundles.

Not here.

• Technical SEO or blog content strategy -> 05-SEO

• Automated email marketing flows -> 09-EML

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Details specific, recurring UX and copywriting mistakes that depress conversion rates across different business models, providing actionable remedies grounded in behavioral psychology and A/B testing data.

modules: [LPG]

topics: [conversion rate optimization, landing page design, e-commerce, B2B lead generation, digital products, above the fold, copywriting, visual hierarchy, FUD reduction, navigation design, bundle pricing]

tier: 3

scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. ad-to-page congruency / explaining that the primary promise in the ad copy (e.g., "Lose 6-20 lbs") must be mirrored exactly in the landing page headline, preventing the immediate bounce caused by generic messaging; optimizing B2B and lead-gen pages / breaking down the ideal above-the-fold structure: benefit-driven headline, descriptive sub-headline, stacked social proof, FUD reducers (Fear, Uncertainty, Doubt), and a conversion-focused CTA (e.g., "Lose Fat Fast" instead of "Contact Us"); removing navigation leaks / advising the removal of top navigation bars (About, Explore, Blog) on dedicated landing pages to force users toward the primary conversion event; the Problem-Agitate-Solve (PAS) framework / structuring mid-page copy to identify the user's struggle, agitate the emotional pain, and present the product as the exact solution; selling digital products and courses / shifting from a transactional feature list (e.g., "5 hours of video") to an outcome-driven offer ("Land six-figure gigs"), utilizing "Value Stacking" to assign monetary worth to bonuses and modules to make the price feel like a no-brainer; optimizing e-commerce homepages / identifying the "View Product Rate" as the most critical homepage metric and prioritizing visual navigation (using icons/images for categories) while keeping menu items under seven to prevent analysis paralysis; e-commerce product page (PDP) fixes / exposing image thumbnails (avoiding hidden dots), placing reviews above the product title, keeping the "Add to Cart" and FUD reducers (warranties, free shipping) above the fold, and explicit bundle savings (e.g., "Save $20" in the bundle title so users don't have to do math); skimmable design / transforming dense paragraphs of product information into visual, icon-driven infographics to accommodate the 80% of users who scan rather than read.

Look for.

Ad-to-Page Congruency: The strict CRO rule that the exact quantifiable promise made in the ad creative must be the very first thing the user reads in the landing page headline.

The "Value Stacking" Framework: A pricing presentation strategy for digital products where every module and bonus is assigned a specific dollar value, making the final bundled price appear heavily discounted.

The "Don't Make Them Do Math" Rule: The pricing psychology tactic of explicitly stating the exact dollar amount saved in the headline of a product bundle (e.g., "3-Pack: Save $20") rather than just showing the discounted price.

Visual Navigation Menus: The UX strategy for e-commerce of replacing text-only drop-down menus with images or icons representing the product categories, which significantly increases click-through rates to product pages.
